```{r setup1, include=FALSE}
# Required packages
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(lubridate)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)
library(tm)
library(SnowballC)
library(igraph)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  fig.align = "center",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4
)

set.seed(3020)

# Approximate event reference time
event_time <- ymd_hms(
  "2026-02-09 01:00:00",
  tz = "UTC"
)

window_days <- 6

# Check required input files
data_dir <- "C:/Users/Admin/OneDrive/COMP3020 (VN)/RStudio WSU VN/Data"

stopifnot(
  file.exists(file.path(data_dir, "posts_clean.csv")),
  file.exists(file.path(data_dir, "collection_log.csv"))
)

md_safe <- function(x) {
  x <- iconv(gsub("\\s+", " ", x), "UTF-8", "ASCII", sub = "")
  gsub("([\\[\\]\\\\`*_{}#$%&~^<>|])", "\\\\\\1", x, perl = TRUE)
}
```

# Data collection

```{r load}
# Load collected posts
posts_all <- read_csv(
  file.path(data_dir, "posts_clean.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  mutate(
    created_at = as_datetime(created_at, tz = "UTC"),
    period = factor(period, levels = c("Before", "After"))
  )

# Keep English-language posts
posts <- posts_all |>
  filter(str_detect(coalesce(langs, ""), "\\ben\\b"))

# Check post counts
c(
  all = nrow(posts_all),
  english = nrow(posts)
)

# Load collection log
collection_log <- read_csv(
  file.path(data_dir, "collection_log.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  mutate(
    capped = capped | n_returned >= 900
  )
```

We collected all the posts via Bluesky API app.bsky.feed.searchPosts (access with app password) using 2 keywords "Bad Bunny" and "halftime how" on 6 Nov 2026. This event is Bad Bunny's Super Bowl halftime show on 8 Feb 2026. This is the reason why this report utilising 6 days long before and after periods is on 01/02/2026, Bad Bunny has won Grammy's Album of the Year, which may dilute the viral moment of the dataset. The kick-off was at 18:30 ET, so the show began around 8:00 ET, which is 1:00 UTC 09/02/2026. Every query was run for each 6 hours separately, up to 10 pages of 100 results per slice, 1 second pause between requests and automatic retries on errors of server. There are 28 of 96 slices that reach 10 pages limit, which mostly around the show; therefore, the results in busiest hours may under-counted and the true number is larger than shown in the report. Duplicated results were removed by post URI. There are `r nrow(posts)` English posts in `r nrow(posts_all)` unique posts used in this analysis (`r sum(posts$period == "Before")` Before posts and `r sum(posts$period == "After")` After posts).

There are 5 limitations in this report. First is the keyword search only find posts that use phrases I listed. The halftime start time is approximate base on our research and judgement. The capped slices under count the busiest time. The "English-only" filter may drop some Spanish language interactions, and lastly, all the search results will depend on Bluesky's index.

# Question 1:

## 1a. Subtopic: language debate

```{r q1a}
lang_pattern <- regex(paste("\\bspanish\\b", "\\benglish\\b", "\\blanguages?\\b", "\\btranslat\\w*","\\bsubtitle[sd]?\\b", "\\bcaptions?\\b", "\\bbilingual\\b", "\\bespa(n|\u00f1)ol\\b", "\\bunderstand\\w*\\b",
  sep = "|"), ignore_case = TRUE)

posts <- posts |>
  mutate(subtopic = factor(if_else(str_detect(coalesce(text, ""), lang_pattern), "Subtopic", "No-Subtopic"), levels = c("Subtopic", "No-Subtopic")))
posts |> count(subtopic) |> kable()
```

```{r q1a-validate, eval=FALSE}
# Validation:
validation <- posts |> filter(subtopic == "Subtopic") |>
  slice_sample(n = 50) |> select(uri, text)
write_csv(validation, "data/lang_validation_sample.csv")
# Precision = share of tagged posts that are really about language
mean(read_csv("data/lang_validation_sample.csv")$is_lang)
```

> **Interpretation:** Bad Bunny's Super Bowl halftime show is main topic and the language debate is our subtopic. This show was performed entirely in Spanish, which became one of the most discussed topic with various comments that they could not understand it and some againts this side. A post was classified as Subtopic post when its post includes at least one of related keyword in this list (Spanish, English, language(s), translat-, subtitle(s), caption(s), bilingual, español, understand), match with both normal words and capitalization word. All other posts including posts with no text were classified as No-Subtopic posts. The outcome from the code is 2,668 Subtopic posts out of 36,556 English posts (only accounted for 7.3%).

To check whether our rule is worked, we manually read a random sample of 50 Subtopic posts. And the results is 47 posts were genuinely about the language of the show (which is 94% precision). The misclassified posts mostly used "understand" in non-language sense, not about language (e.g. "a choice that I truly can't understand"). The rule also miss language-related posts that not use any keyword in our list; therefore, the correct number of language post may higher than our outcome.

## 1b. Chi-square test

- H0: Subtopic status is independent of time period. The percentage of language-debate posts is the same for before and after show.

- H1: Subtopic status is associated with time period.

```{r q1b}
tab <- table(Period = posts$period, Subtopic = posts$subtopic)
kable(addmargins(tab), caption = "Observed counts")
kable(round(prop.table(tab, 1), 3), caption = "Row proportions")

expected <- outer(rowSums(tab), colSums(tab)) / sum(tab)
kable(round(expected, 1), caption = "Expected counts under H0")

chi_manual <- sum((tab - expected)^2 / expected)   # sum of (O - E)^2 / E
test <- chisq.test(tab, correct = FALSE)
chi_manual
test
```

> **Interpretation:** Table 1 demonstrates the observed counts, table 3 shows the expected counts under H0. Before the show, there are 733 of 15,435 posts discussed about language (which accounted for only 4.7%). But after the show, this percentage rose to 9.2%, almost doubled the number before with 1,935 out of 21,121 posts. The chi-square test provides χ² = 256.64 (df = 1, p \< 0.001), a sign to reject H0 ar 5% level. A post discuessed language will depend on whether it was posted before or after the show. The outcome clearly shows that a performance using entirely Spanish turned language into a larger concern in the conservation. Before the show, language is just an expected issue. But after the show, it become the center of praise and criticism.

## 1c. Twitter's chi-square score

Twitter's chi-square score in this solution compared observed with expected frequencies based on historical data. The before-show is the baseline in this analysis. Because the two period before and after show contain different post numbers, the historical proportions are adjusted to the sample size of after event.

```{r q1c}
# Original counts from Question 1(b)
before_topic <- 733
before_total <- 15435

after_topic <- 1935
after_total <- 21121

# Calculate non-subtopic posts
before_no_topic <- before_total - before_topic
after_no_topic <- after_total - after_topic

# Expected after-event counts based on before-event proportions
expected_topic <- after_total * before_topic / before_total
expected_no_topic <- after_total * before_no_topic / before_total

# Twitter's historical-baseline chi-square score
twitter_chi <- 
  (after_topic - expected_topic)^2 / expected_topic +
  (after_no_topic - expected_no_topic)^2 / expected_no_topic

# Pearson chi-square test for comparison
contingency <- matrix(
  c(
    before_topic, before_no_topic,
    after_topic, after_no_topic
  ),
  nrow = 2,
  byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(
    Period = c("Before", "After"),
    Status = c("Subtopic", "No-Subtopic")
  )
)

pearson_chi <- chisq.test(
  contingency,
  correct = FALSE
)$statistic

# Display results
comparison <- data.frame(
  Method = c(
    "Pearson chi-square",
    "Twitter historical-baseline chi-square"
  ),
  Chi_square = c(
    unname(pearson_chi),
    twitter_chi
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  comparison,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Comparison of Pearson and Twitter Chi-square Scores"
)
```

> **Interpretation:** Twitter's chi-square score measures the change in the number of language-related posts between before and after Bad Bunny's Super Bowl halftime show. Using the historical proportion as baseline, Twitter's chi square score indicate a dramatic grow in language discssuion. The difference between Pearson and Twitter occurs is because Twitter treats historical distribution as fixed while Person estimates expected frequencies using both periods (before and after show). So the Pearson will provide more appropriate results for testing statistical independence, whereas Twitter will assess the departure from historical topic frequencies.

## 1d. Linear trend in daily post counts

We used 12 consecutive 24-hour periods, six days before and six days after the event (12 complete and equal days from -6 to 5). We used simple linear regression to assess because this provides us whether the number of language-related posts about the show changed linearly overtime.

We built a linear regression with dependent variable is daily English post counts on day related to show (days -6 to 5).

### Daily post counts

```{r q1d-daily-counts}
# Use the cleaned English-language posts from question 1a
# event_time and window_days are defined in the setup

daily <- posts |>
  mutate(
    day = floor(
      as.numeric(
        difftime(
          created_at,
          event_time,
          units = "days"
        )
      )
    )
  ) |>
  filter(
    day >= -window_days,
    day < window_days
  ) |>
  count(day, name = "n") |>
  tidyr::complete(
    day = seq(
      -window_days,
      window_days - 1
    ),
    fill = list(n = 0)
  ) |>
  arrange(day)

# Display daily counts
knitr::kable(
  daily,
  col.names = c(
    "Day Relative to Event",
    "Number of English Posts"
  ),
  caption = "Table 4. Daily Bluesky Post Counts"
)
```

### Linear regression model

```{r q1d-regression}
fit <- lm(n ~ day, data = daily) # Fit a simple linear regression model

summary(fit) # Display regression results

# Extract model statistics
slope <- unname(coef(fit)["day"])

r_squared <- summary(fit)$r.squared

adjusted_r2 <- summary(fit)$adj.r.squared

p_value <- summary(fit)$coefficients[
  "day", "Pr(>|t|)"
]

# Create a summary table
regression_results <- data.frame(
  Metric = c(
    "Slope",
    "R-squared",
    "Adjusted R-squared",
    "Slope p-value"
  ),
  Value = c(
    slope,
    r_squared,
    adjusted_r2,
    p_value
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  regression_results,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Table 5. Linear Regression Results"
)
```

### Scatter plot & Fitted regression line

```{r q1d-plot, fig.cap="Figure 1. Daily Bluesky post counts and fitted linear regression line."}
ggplot(daily, aes(x = day, y = n)) +
  geom_point(
    size = 3,
    color = "#2563A6"
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = TRUE,
    color = "#D1495B",
    fill = "#F4A6AE",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = -0.5,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "grey40"
  ) +
  ggplot2::annotate(
    "text",
    x = 0,
    y = max(daily$n),
    label = "Halftime show",
    hjust = 0,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = -window_days:(window_days - 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Daily Bluesky Posts About Bad Bunny's Halftime Show",
    subtitle = "Simple linear regression across 12 days",
    x = "Day Relative to Halftime Show",
    y = "Number of English Posts per Day"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

> **Interpretation:**

The positive slope is 72.3 means that there is an increase of about 72 posts per additional day accross observation period. However, this slope is not statistically significant due to p = 0.59 and the standard error of 129.7 is larger than the slope, which indicate insufficient evidence of consistent linear trend.

The R-squared value R² = 0.03 means that time explains only 3% of the variation in daily posts. The negative adjusted R² = -0.0669 means that the performance of this model worse after accounting for the predictor.

The data illustrate a rocket, when the number of posts is around 1,581 to 2,288 per day until three days before the show, increase to 4,774 on D-1, reach the highest point at 5,412 on D-day (3.4 times the quietest day), and decreased to 1,576 after 5 days. This pattern illustrate a temporary increase in discussion rather than increase consistently over time.

Therefore, the model does not suggest a linear trend.

## 1e. Limitations of a linear regression

Simple linear regression assumes constant change rate over time. But the way social media work does not follow a constant flow. Its engagement depends on events, which means it will increases dramatically around major events and declines after that. With this working flow, the straight regression line cannot represent for social media engagements.

### Residual analysis

```{r q1e, fig.height=4}
# Use the daily counts and regression model from Question 1d

residual_data <- data.frame(
  day = daily$day,
  residual = resid(fit)
)

# Plot regression residuals
ggplot(
  residual_data,
  aes(x = day, y = residual)
) +
  geom_col(
    fill = "#457B9D",
    width = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "grey30"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = -window_days:(window_days - 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals of the Linear Regression Model",
    x = "Day Relative to Halftime Show",
    y = "Residual (Observed - Predicted Posts)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

> **Interpretation:**

The residual plot shows a systematic pattern rather than random noise. The regression line overestimated both ends of the period post counts (residual decreases to -1,868 on day 5) and underestimated the days near the performance (positive residual up to +2,330 on day 0).

Next, this pattern happens since the "viral" effect follows the shape rise-peak-decline that a straight line cannot follow. A straight regression line assumes constant change so it cannot represent a sudden increase in attention and then declined. For example, some peak days dominate the fit so that the regression pulled upward.

Moreover, the linear regression go with the assumption independent observations; however, the social media activity on one day can strongly depends on various influences from the previous day, and it can predict impossible negative counts if extended.

There are 28 search slices reached the API page limit, so the observed peak may under-counted, in the other word, it means the true spike is even sharper. Some posts might have been missed, especially during high activity time.

Some alternative approaches, for example, the interrupted time-series model (allowing different levels before and after event) or a count model like Poisson regression would better examining changes related to event like viral moment.

Overall, the low R-square (0.0301) and the systematic residual pattern demonstrate a simple linear refgression provides poor description of this viral event.

## 2a. The three most-replied posts

top3 <- read_csv("data/top3_posts.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
top3 |>

Each post and all of its replies (including replies to replies) form one discussion thread, retrieved with `app.bsky.feed.getPostThread`.

```{r q2a-counts}
replies <- read_csv("data/replies.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
replies |> count(thread, name = "Replies retrieved") |>
  left_join(top3 |> select(thread, `Reply count on post` = reply_count), by = "thread") |>
  kable()

> **Interpretation:** As seen in the table, the number of replies retrieved successfully in T1, T2 and T3 (285, 298, and 309 respectively) is much shorter than those that appeared in the public posts (691, 662 and 640 respectively), with only between 41% and 48% of the replies appearing in the public posts actually being retrieved. There are multiple structural and moderation reasons to this data loss in social web analytics that is experienced commonly. In particular, users often remove their own posts (particularly from polarized threads such as T1 and T3), and the platforms are moderated to hide toxic and abusive comments from the public view. Additionally, when users use their private accounts or block the collector's interaction, it will be hidden from the general public.
>
> The total volume is therefore lower than what is shown on the platform, but this data is not accessible, and thus forms a natural filter. The 892 retrieved replies in the resulting sample are a more representative, high-quality and publicly visible discourse for our text mining.

## 2b. Word frequencies per thread

```{r q2b}
# Topic words appear in almost every reply, so they are removed to let themes show;
# contractions lose their apostrophe after punctuation removal, hence "dont", "im".
custom_stop <- c("bad", "bunny", "badbunny", "benito", "halftime", "show",
                 "super", "bowl", "superbowl", "nfl",
                 "just", "like", "get", "will", "can", "one", "also", "really",
                 "dont", "im", "its", "ive", "youre", "thats", "cant", "doesnt",
                 "isnt", "amp")

clean_corpus <- function(text, stem = FALSE) {
  text <- gsub("[\u2018\u2019]", "'", text)                  # curly apostrophes
  text <- iconv(text, "UTF-8", "ASCII", sub = " ")          # drop emoji
  corp <- VCorpus(VectorSource(text))
  corp <- tm_map(corp, content_transformer(tolower))
  corp <- tm_map(corp, content_transformer(function(x) gsub("https?://\\S+|www\\.\\S+", " ", x)))
  corp <- tm_map(corp, content_transformer(function(x) gsub("@\\S+", " ", x)))
  corp <- tm_map(corp, removeWords, stopwords("english"))
  corp <- tm_map(corp, removePunctuation)
  corp <- tm_map(corp, removeNumbers)
  corp <- tm_map(corp, removeWords, custom_stop)
  if (stem) corp <- tm_map(corp, stemDocument)
  tm_map(corp, stripWhitespace)
}

freq <- lapply(split(replies$text, replies$thread), function(txt) {
  tdm <- TermDocumentMatrix(clean_corpus(txt))   # default keeps words of 3+ letters
  f <- sort(rowSums(as.matrix(tdm)), decreasing = TRUE)
  tibble(word = names(f), freq = as.integer(f))
}) |> bind_rows(.id = "thread")

top15 <- freq |> group_by(thread) |>
  slice_max(freq, n = 15, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  mutate(rank = row_number()) |> ungroup()

top15 |> mutate(entry = paste0(word, " (", freq, ")")) |>
  select(rank, thread, entry) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = thread, values_from = entry) |>
  kable(caption = "Top 15 words per thread (frequency)")
```

```{r q2b-chart, fig.height=5}
ggplot(top15, aes(freq, reorder(paste(word, thread, sep = "___"), freq))) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ thread, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = function(x) sub("___.*", "", x)) +
  labs(x = "Frequency", y = NULL, title = "Top 15 words in the replies of each thread")
```

## 2c. Themes

> **Interpretation** The themes and words used in the original post were heavily influenced by the angle taken in the reply thread which is revealed by an analysis of the top words.
>
> Thread 1 (Political News Angle): Sparked by a politician's investigation of the show, the main themes are Political Controversy and the Language Debate. The discussion is very polarized and politically loaded with aggressive vocabulary ("alford", "epstein", "maga", "pathetic", "fucking") mixed with words specific to the language being used ("spanish", "lyrics").
>
> Thread 2 (Wholesome Anecdote Angle): Themes change completely as it is based on a story of a 70-year-old father. The words are all positive and nostalgic - "dad", "music", "righteous", "brothers", "love", "loved", "great". Though the language barrier is a theme ("understand", "spanish", "words"), they are not made into a problem that is solved by the performance's energy.
>
> Thread 3 (Political Opinion Angle): Given an invitation to criticize the opposing party that is offered by right wing outrage, the key themes are Partisan Criticism and Chronic Outrage. There is not a lot of discussion about the halftime show itself, but rather about the meta-commentary on how conservative they have been, such as "right", "complain", "complained", "white", "always", and "years".
>
> When comparing the threads, both Thread 1 and Thread 3 are very political and critical (for instance: "maga" in Thread 1, "right/complain" in Thread 3), while Thread 2 is completely different, which demostrates a wholesome approach to musical pleasure. Moreover, the separate collection of terms indicates that users are often reflecting the framing of the original author, whether it is a political threat, a happy moment or a partisan critique. Finally, the difference between the two sets of vocabulary shows that users are closely following the original author's lines of thought, as in either case "spanish" is a key word.

## Introduction

This part of the project looks at comments from the three Bluesky threads selected in Question 2 about Bad Bunny's Super Bowl halftime show.

I combined the comments into one dataset and used TF-IDF to represent their text. I then used K-means clustering to group comments with similar vocabulary.

To decide how many clusters to use, I compared average silhouette scores for different values of k. After clustering, I used a two-dimensional plot to show the results and compared the clusters with the original threads.

I also included a short supplementary analysis to check how removing comments with limited vocabulary affects the clustering results.

## Data Collection

The comments were collected from Bluesky using the `atrrr` package in R. The three selected threads were labelled T1, T2 and T3.

Each reply contains a unique URI, its original thread label and the comment text. The collected data was saved as `Data/replies.csv`.

I used the saved CSV file for the analysis, so there was no need to connect to Bluesky again.

### Bluesky Authentication

During data collection, I used a Bluesky account and an app password to access the API. The credentials are not included in this report.

The authentication code is shown below for reference and is not run when knitting the document.

```{r q3-bluesky-auth, eval=FALSE}
library(atrrr)

atrrr::auth(
  user = Sys.getenv("BLUESKY_USER"),
  password = Sys.getenv("BLUESKY_APP_PASSWORD")
)
```

## Load the Dataset

I used `tidyverse` for data cleaning and plots, `tidytext` for text processing and TF-IDF, `Matrix` for the sparse document-term matrix, `cluster` for silhouette analysis and `irlba` for the two-dimensional visualisation.

```{r q3-load-replies}
replies <- read_csv(
  file.path(data_dir, "replies.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

stopifnot(
  all(c("uri", "thread", "text") %in% names(replies)),
  nrow(replies) > 0
)

data_overview <- replies %>%
  summarise(
    total_comments = n(),
    total_threads = n_distinct(thread, na.rm = TRUE),
    unique_comments = n_distinct(uri, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

knitr::kable(
  data_overview,
  caption = "Overview of collected comments"
)
```

The dataset contains `r nrow(replies)` comments from `r n_distinct(replies$thread, na.rm = TRUE)` threads, with `r n_distinct(replies$uri, na.rm = TRUE)` unique non-missing comment IDs.

Before clustering, I cleaned the text, removed duplicate comments and converted the remaining words into TF-IDF values.

# Question 3. Clustering and Visualisation

This question uses comments from the three Bluesky threads selected in Question 2. I used TF-IDF to represent the comment text and K-means clustering to group comments based on their vocabulary. I then visualised the clusters and compared them with the original thread labels to see whether comments from the same thread were grouped together.

## Question 3a. Text Preprocessing and TF-IDF Document Term Matrix

### Purpose of the Analysis

The comments from T1, T2 and T3 were combined into one dataset. I cleaned the text and calculated TF-IDF values to create a Document Term Matrix (DTM). Each row represents a comment, while each column represents a word. This matrix was then used for the clustering analysis in Questions 3(b) and 3(c).

### 1. Load and Examine the Collected Comments

I loaded the comments from Data/replies.csv, which was collected in Question 2. Before processing the text, I checked the number of comments in each thread, missing values, duplicate comment IDs and comment lengths.

```{r q3a-load-data, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Load required packages
library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)
library(Matrix)
library(cluster)
library(knitr)

# Load the collected comments
replies <- readr::read_csv(
  "Data/replies.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Verify required columns
stopifnot(
  all(
    c("uri", "text", "thread") %in%
      names(replies)
  ),
  nrow(replies) > 0
)

# Count collected comments by original thread
thread_counts <- replies %>%
  count(
    thread,
    name = "n_replies"
  )

knitr::kable(
  thread_counts,
  caption = "Number of collected comments by original thread"
)
```

### 2. Assess Data Quality

I checked the dataset for missing text, empty comments and duplicate comment IDs. I also looked at comment lengths to compare the amount of text available from each thread.

```{r q3a-data-quality}
# Check missing values and duplicate identifiers
data_quality <- replies %>%
  summarise(
    total_replies = n(),
    missing_uri = sum(is.na(uri) | trimws(uri) == ""),
    missing_thread = sum(
      is.na(thread) | trimws(thread) == ""
    ),
    missing_text = sum(is.na(text)),
    empty_text = sum(
      is.na(text) |
        trimws(replace_na(text, "")) == ""
    ),
    duplicate_uris = sum(
      duplicated(uri) & !is.na(uri)
    )
  )

knitr::kable(
  data_quality,
  caption = "Initial data quality assessment"
)

# Summarise original comment lengths by thread
text_lengths <- replies %>%
  mutate(
    text_length = nchar(
      replace_na(text, "")
    )
  ) %>%
  group_by(thread) %>%
  summarise(
    n_comments = n(),
    mean_length = round(
      mean(text_length),
      2
    ),
    median_length = median(text_length),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

knitr::kable(
  text_lengths,
  caption = "Comment length statistics by original thread"
)
```

### 3. Preprocess the Comment Text

The following preprocessing steps were applied:

1.  Remove comments with missing identifiers, thread labels, or empty text.
2.  Remove duplicate comments using their unique URI.
3.  Convert the text to lowercase.
4.  Tokenise comments into individual words.
5.  Remove punctuation, numbers, and common English stop words.
6.  Retain alphabetic tokens containing at least three characters.

Only words containing at least three letters were kept. The token filter `^[a-z]+$` also removes words with accented characters, so some Spanish words may have been excluded from the analysis.

```{r q3a-preprocessing, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Verify that thread labels match the three selected threads
valid_threads <- c("T1", "T2", "T3")

invalid_threads <- replies %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(thread),
    trimws(thread) != "",
    !thread %in% valid_threads
  )

stopifnot(
  nrow(invalid_threads) == 0
)

# Remove invalid and duplicate comments
comments <- replies %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(uri),
    trimws(uri) != "",
    !is.na(thread),
    thread %in% valid_threads,
    !is.na(text),
    stringr::str_trim(text) != ""
  ) %>%
  distinct(
    uri,
    .keep_all = TRUE
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    comment_id = as.character(uri),
    thread = factor(
      thread,
      levels = valid_threads
    ),
    text = stringr::str_to_lower(text)
  )

# Verify cleaned comment identifiers
stopifnot(
  nrow(comments) > 0,
  !anyNA(comments$comment_id),
  !anyDuplicated(comments$comment_id),
  !anyNA(comments$thread)
)

# Load English stop words
data("stop_words", package = "tidytext")

# Tokenise and clean the comments
tokens <- comments %>%
  select(
    comment_id,
    thread,
    text
  ) %>%
  tidytext::unnest_tokens(
    word,
    text
  ) %>%
  filter(
    stringr::str_detect(
      word,
      "^[a-z]+$"
    )
  ) %>%
  anti_join(
    tidytext::stop_words,
    by = "word"
  ) %>%
  filter(
    nchar(word) >= 3
  )

# Count occurrences of each word within each comment
word_counts <- tokens %>%
  count(
    comment_id,
    word,
    name = "n"
  )

# Verify that terms remain after preprocessing
stopifnot(
  nrow(word_counts) > 0
)

# Summarise preprocessing
preprocessing_summary <- tibble(
  Measure = c(
    "Original collected comments",
    "Comments after validation and deduplication",
    "Comments removed before tokenisation",
    "Comments with retained vocabulary",
    "Unique retained terms"
  ),
  Value = c(
    nrow(replies),
    nrow(comments),
    nrow(replies) - nrow(comments),
    n_distinct(word_counts$comment_id),
    n_distinct(word_counts$word)
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  preprocessing_summary,
  caption = "Summary of comment preprocessing"
)
```

### 4. Calculate TF-IDF Weights

I used TF-IDF to measure how important each word was in a comment compared with the other comments in the dataset.

TF-IDF is calculated as:

$$
TFIDF(t,d) = TF(t,d) \times IDF(t)
$$

The term frequency is:

$$
TF(t,d) =
\frac{f(t,d)}
{\sum_{w} f(w,d)}
$$

where $f(t,d)$ is the number of occurrences of term $t$ in document $d$, and the denominator is the total number of retained word occurrences in document $d$.

Inverse document frequency is:

$$
IDF(t) =
\ln\left(\frac{N}{df(t)}\right)
$$

where:

- $N$ is the number of documents containing at least one retained term.
- $df(t)$ is the number of documents containing term $t$.
- $\ln$ denotes the natural logarithm.

I used the `bind_tf_idf()` function from the `tidytext` package to calculate these values. Words appearing in fewer comments receive higher IDF weights, while words found in every retained document receive an IDF of zero.

```{r q3a-tfidf}
# Calculate TF-IDF weights
tfidf_data <- word_counts %>%
  tidytext::bind_tf_idf(
    word,
    comment_id,
    n
  )

# Verify calculated weights
stopifnot(
  nrow(tfidf_data) > 0,
  all(is.finite(tfidf_data$tf_idf)),
  all(tfidf_data$tf_idf >= 0)
)

# Display the ten highest TF-IDF term-document pairs
top_tfidf <- tfidf_data %>%
  arrange(
    desc(tf_idf)
  ) %>%
  slice_head(
    n = 10
  ) %>%
  select(
    comment_id,
    word,
    n,
    tf,
    idf,
    tf_idf
  )

knitr::kable(
  top_tfidf,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Ten highest TF-IDF term-document weights"
)
```

### 5. Construct the Document Term Matrix

I converted the TF-IDF values into a sparse Document Term Matrix (DTM). Each row represents a comment, each column represents a word, and the values show the corresponding TF-IDF weights.

I used a sparse matrix because most comments contain only a small number of words from the full vocabulary. Comments without retained words were excluded during matrix construction. I also removed rows with zero TF-IDF magnitude because these vectors cannot be L2-normalised for clustering.

```{r q3a-dtm}
# Construct the sparse TF-IDF Document Term Matrix
dtm <- tfidf_data %>%
  tidytext::cast_sparse(
    comment_id,
    word,
    tf_idf
  )

# Count documents before removing zero vectors
dtm_rows_before <- nrow(dtm)

# Identify nonzero TF-IDF document vectors
nonzero_rows <- Matrix::rowSums(
  dtm^2
) > 0

# Remove zero-magnitude document vectors
dtm <- dtm[
  nonzero_rows,
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

# Remove vocabulary columns with no remaining weights
dtm <- dtm[
  ,
  Matrix::colSums(dtm != 0) > 0,
  drop = FALSE
]

# Verify final DTM
stopifnot(
  nrow(dtm) > 0,
  ncol(dtm) > 0,
  !is.null(rownames(dtm)),
  !anyDuplicated(rownames(dtm)),
  all(Matrix::rowSums(dtm^2) > 0)
)

# Calculate exclusion counts
comments_without_terms <- nrow(comments) -
  n_distinct(word_counts$comment_id)

zero_vector_comments <- dtm_rows_before -
  nrow(dtm)

# Summarise final matrix
dtm_summary <- tibble(
  Measure = c(
    "Comments after validation and deduplication",
    "Comments without retained terms",
    "Comments with zero TF-IDF vectors",
    "Final documents",
    "Final vocabulary terms",
    "Nonzero matrix entries"
  ),
  Value = c(
    nrow(comments),
    comments_without_terms,
    zero_vector_comments,
    nrow(dtm),
    ncol(dtm),
    Matrix::nnzero(dtm)
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  dtm_summary,
  caption = "Final TF-IDF Document Term Matrix summary"
)
```

### 6. Preserve Original Thread Labels

I kept the original thread labels (T1, T2 and T3) so I could compare them with the clusters later in Questions 3(d) and 3(e). I also matched the comment IDs to the row order of the TF-IDF matrix to make sure each comment had the correct thread label.

```{r q3a-metadata}
# Match original metadata to final DTM rows
comment_metadata <- comments %>%
  select(
    comment_id,
    thread
  ) %>%
  slice(
    match(
      rownames(dtm),
      comment_id
    )
  )

# Verify exact alignment
stopifnot(
  nrow(comment_metadata) == nrow(dtm),
  !anyNA(comment_metadata$comment_id),
  !anyNA(comment_metadata$thread),
  identical(
    as.character(comment_metadata$comment_id),
    rownames(dtm)
  )
)

# Summarise retained comments by thread
retained_thread_counts <- comment_metadata %>%
  count(
    thread,
    name = "n_comments",
    .drop = FALSE
  )

knitr::kable(
  retained_thread_counts,
  caption = "Final retained comments by original thread"
)
```

### 7. Save the Preprocessing Results

The TF-IDF weights, document metadata, and sparse Document Term Matrix were saved for reproducibility and use in subsequent questions.

```{r q3a-save-results, include=FALSE}
# Save TF-IDF weights
readr::write_csv(
  tfidf_data,
  "Data/q3_tfidf.csv"
)

# Save aligned comment metadata
readr::write_csv(
  comment_metadata,
  "Data/q3_comment_metadata.csv"
)

# Save sparse TF-IDF matrix
saveRDS(
  dtm,
  "Data/q3_dtm.rds"
)

# Verify saved files
stopifnot(
  file.exists("Data/q3_tfidf.csv"),
  file.exists("Data/q3_comment_metadata.csv"),
  file.exists("Data/q3_dtm.rds")
)
```

### **Interpretation**

> The original dataset contained `r nrow(replies)` comments from the three Bluesky threads. After removing missing records and duplicate IDs, `r nrow(comments)` comments remained. During text preprocessing, `r comments_without_terms` comments were excluded because they had no retained words. Another `r zero_vector_comments` comments were removed because their TF-IDF vectors had zero magnitude. The final TF-IDF matrix contained `r nrow(dtm)` comments and `r ncol(dtm)` vocabulary terms, with `r Matrix::nnzero(dtm)` nonzero values. Each row represents a comment, while the columns represent the words found in the dataset. The TF-IDF values show how important each word is relative to the other comments. I used this matrix for clustering in Questions 3(b) and 3(c). The original thread labels were kept separately for the visualisation and comparison in Questions 3(d) and 3(e).

## Question 3b. Determining the Optimal Number of Clusters

### Purpose of the Analysis

I used the TF-IDF matrix from Question 3(a) to find a suitable number of clusters for the combined comments. I tested values from $k=2$ to $k=10$ and compared their average silhouette scores using cosine distance. The value of $k$ with the highest average score was selected.

### 1. Normalise the TF-IDF Document Vectors

Before clustering, I converted the TF-IDF matrix into a numerical matrix and normalised each comment vector to have a length of 1.

For document vector $\mathbf{x}_i$, L2 normalisation is defined as:

$$
\mathbf{x}_i^* =
\frac{\mathbf{x}_i}{\|\mathbf{x}_i\|_2}
$$

where $\|\mathbf{x}_i\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm of the original TF-IDF vector.

I used normalisation to reduce the effect of differences in vector length and focus more on the relative TF-IDF weights of the words.

```{r q3b-normalisation, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Convert the sparse TF-IDF matrix into a numerical matrix
X <- as.matrix(dtm)

# Preserve original comment identifiers
stopifnot(
  !is.null(rownames(X)),
  identical(rownames(X), rownames(dtm))
)

# Calculate the Euclidean norm of each document vector
row_lengths <- sqrt(
  rowSums(X^2)
)

# Confirm all document vectors have nonzero magnitude
stopifnot(
  all(is.finite(row_lengths)),
  all(row_lengths > 0)
)

# Apply L2 normalisation
X_norm <- sweep(
  X,
  1,
  row_lengths,
  FUN = "/"
)

# Verify unit-length vectors
normalised_lengths <- sqrt(
  rowSums(X_norm^2)
)

stopifnot(
  all(abs(normalised_lengths - 1) < 1e-8),
  identical(rownames(X_norm), rownames(dtm))
)

# Summarise the normalised matrix
normalisation_summary <- tibble(
  Measure = c(
    "Number of comments",
    "Number of TF-IDF features",
    "Minimum normalised vector length",
    "Maximum normalised vector length"
  ),
  Value = c(
    as.character(nrow(X_norm)),
    as.character(ncol(X_norm)),
    sprintf("%.6f", min(normalised_lengths)),
    sprintf("%.6f", max(normalised_lengths))
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  normalisation_summary,
  caption = "Summary of L2-normalised TF-IDF vectors"
)
```

### 2. Calculate Cosine Distances

I used cosine distance to compare the vocabulary patterns between comments.

For two L2-normalised document vectors, cosine distance is calculated as:

$$
d_{\cos}(i,j) =
1-\mathbf{x}_i^{*T}\mathbf{x}_j^*
$$

A smaller distance means the comments have more similar TF-IDF representations.

I chose cosine distance because the analysis focuses on similarities in word usage rather than the original lengths of the document vectors.

K-means uses squared Euclidean distance to form clusters. I used cosine distance separately when calculating silhouette scores to evaluate the resulting clusters.

```{r q3b-cosine-distance}
# Calculate pairwise cosine distances
cosine_distance_matrix <- 1 - tcrossprod(X_norm)

# Correct minor numerical rounding errors
cosine_distance_matrix <- pmax(
  cosine_distance_matrix,
  0
)

# Ensure a zero diagonal and matrix symmetry
cosine_distance_matrix <- (
  cosine_distance_matrix +
    t(cosine_distance_matrix)
) / 2

diag(cosine_distance_matrix) <- 0

# Convert the matrix into a distance object
cosine_dist <- stats::as.dist(
  cosine_distance_matrix
)

# Verify calculated distances
stopifnot(
  all(is.finite(cosine_distance_matrix)),
  all(cosine_distance_matrix >= 0),
  max(
    abs(
      cosine_distance_matrix -
        t(cosine_distance_matrix)
    )
  ) < 1e-8
)
```

### 3. Evaluate Candidate Cluster Numbers

I used silhouette scores to check how well the comments were grouped for each value of (k). The score compares how close a comment is to others in its own cluster with how close it is to comments in the nearest alternative cluster.

For observation $i$, the silhouette coefficient is:

$$
s(i) =
\frac{b(i)-a(i)}
{\max(a(i),b(i))}
$$

where:

- $a(i)$ is the average distance between observation $i$ and other observations in its assigned cluster.
- $b(i)$ is the minimum average distance between observation $i$ and observations in another cluster.

The average silhouette score for (k) clusters is:

$$
\bar{s}(k) =
\frac{1}{N}
\sum_{i=1}^{N}s(i)
$$

where $N$ represents the total number of comments.

Silhouette scores range from -1 to 1. A positive score suggests a comment fits better in its assigned cluster. Scores close to zero indicate weak separation between clusters, while negative scores suggest the comment is closer to another cluster.

I tested nine values of $k$, from $k=2$ to $k=10$.

For each value, I ran K-means with 25 random starts, a maximum of 300 iterations and a random seed of 42.

```{r q3b-cluster-evaluation, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Define candidate numbers of clusters
k_values <- 2:10

# Verify the dataset supports the candidate range
stopifnot(
  nrow(X_norm) > max(k_values)
)

# Count distinct normalised document vectors
n_distinct_vectors <- nrow(
  unique(
    as.data.frame(X_norm)
  )
)

stopifnot(
  n_distinct_vectors >= max(k_values)
)

# Evaluate K-means solutions using cosine silhouettes
silhouette_results <- purrr::map_dfr(
  k_values,
  function(k) {

    set.seed(42)

    model <- stats::kmeans(
      X_norm,
      centers = k,
      nstart = 25,
      iter.max = 300
    )

    # Calculate cosine-distance silhouette coefficients
    sil <- cluster::silhouette(
      model$cluster,
      cosine_dist
    )

    tibble(
      k = k,
      avg_silhouette = mean(
        sil[, "sil_width"]
      ),
      total_wss = model$tot.withinss
    )
  }
)

# Verify the evaluation results
stopifnot(
  nrow(silhouette_results) == length(k_values),
  all(is.finite(silhouette_results$avg_silhouette)),
  all(is.finite(silhouette_results$total_wss))
)

# Display candidate results
knitr::kable(
  silhouette_results,
  digits = 4,
  col.names = c(
    "Number of Clusters (k)",
    "Average Silhouette Score",
    "Total Within-Cluster Sum of Squares"
  ),
  caption = "Comparison of candidate K-means clustering solutions"
)
```

### 4. Select the Optimal Number of Clusters

I selected the value of (k) with the highest average silhouette score:

$$
k^* =
\underset{k \in \{2,\ldots,10\}}{\arg\max}
\ \bar{s}(k)
$$

This gives the best-performing number of clusters among the nine values tested. I also compared the highest score with the second-highest score to see how much difference there was between the two solutions.

```{r q3b-select-k}
# Rank candidate solutions by average silhouette score
ranked_results <- silhouette_results %>%
  arrange(
    desc(avg_silhouette),
    k
  )

# Extract the best candidate
best_k <- ranked_results$k[[1]]

best_score <- ranked_results$avg_silhouette[[1]]

# Extract the second-best candidate
second_best_k <- ranked_results$k[[2]]

second_best_score <- ranked_results$avg_silhouette[[2]]

# Calculate the difference between the top two scores
score_difference <- best_score - second_best_score

# Display selection results
selection_summary <- tibble(
  Measure = c(
    "Selected number of clusters",
    "Highest average silhouette score",
    "Second-best number of clusters",
    "Second-highest silhouette score",
    "Difference between top two scores"
  ),
  Value = c(
    as.character(best_k),
    sprintf("%.4f", best_score),
    as.character(second_best_k),
    sprintf("%.4f", second_best_score),
    sprintf("%.4f", score_difference)
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  selection_summary,
  caption = "Optimal cluster selection summary"
)
```

### 5. Visualise the Silhouette Evaluation

The line chart below shows the average silhouette score for each value of $k$ from 2 to 10. The dashed vertical line marks the selected number of clusters.

```{r q3b-silhouette-plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Average cosine-distance silhouette scores for K-means clustering with k = 2 to 10."}
p_silhouette <- ggplot(
  silhouette_results,
  aes(
    x = k,
    y = avg_silhouette
  )
) +
  geom_line(
    linewidth = 0.8,
    colour = "#2563A6"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    size = 2.5,
    colour = "#2563A6"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = best_k,
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "#D1495B"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = silhouette_results %>%
      filter(k == best_k),
    size = 3.5,
    colour = "#D1495B"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = k_values
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Optimal Number of Clusters",
    subtitle = "Average silhouette scores using cosine distance",
    x = "Number of Clusters (k)",
    y = "Average Silhouette Score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

print(p_silhouette)

# Save the figure
ggsave(
  "Data/q3_silhouette_plot.png",
  plot = p_silhouette,
  width = 8,
  height = 5,
  dpi = 300
)
```

### 6. Examine the Selected Solution

After selecting the number of clusters, I checked how many comments had negative silhouette scores. A negative score means a comment is closer, on average, to another cluster than to its assigned cluster.

I also ran K-means again using the selected value of (k), with the same random seed and settings, to check the selected solution.

```{r q3b-selected-diagnostics}
# Refit the selected candidate using identical parameters
set.seed(42)

selected_model <- stats::kmeans(
  X_norm,
  centers = best_k,
  nstart = 25,
  iter.max = 300
)

# Calculate individual silhouette coefficients
selected_silhouette <- cluster::silhouette(
  selected_model$cluster,
  cosine_dist
)

# Summarise the selected solution
selected_avg_silhouette <- mean(
  selected_silhouette[, "sil_width"]
)

negative_silhouette_pct <- 100 * mean(
  selected_silhouette[, "sil_width"] < 0
)

# Verify consistency with the selected score
stopifnot(
  abs(selected_avg_silhouette - best_score) < 1e-8
)

selected_diagnostics <- tibble(
  Measure = c(
    "Selected number of clusters",
    "Average silhouette score",
    "Comments with negative silhouette (%)"
  ),
  Value = c(
    as.character(best_k),
    sprintf("%.4f", selected_avg_silhouette),
    sprintf("%.2f", negative_silhouette_pct)
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  selected_diagnostics,
  caption = "Silhouette diagnostics for the selected solution"
)
```

### 7. Save the Evaluation Results

The silhouette evaluation results were saved for reproducibility and subsequent analysis.

```{r q3b-save-results, include=FALSE}
readr::write_csv(
  silhouette_results,
  "Data/q3_silhouette_results.csv"
)

stopifnot(
  file.exists("Data/q3_silhouette_results.csv"),
  file.exists("Data/q3_silhouette_plot.png")
)
```

### **Interpretation**

> I tested nine clustering solutions, ranging from $k=2$ to $k=10$. The highest average silhouette score was `r round(best_score, 4)`, at $k=`r best_k`$. The second-highest score was `r round(second_best_score, 4)`, at $k=`r second_best_k`$, giving a difference of`r round(score_difference, 4)`. For the selected solution, `r round(negative_silhouette_pct, 2)`% of comments had negative silhouette scores. `r if (best_score > 0.5) {   "The score suggests relatively clear separation between clusters." } else if (best_score > 0.25) {   "The score suggests some separation, although the clusters still overlap." } else {   "The score suggests weak separation, with considerable overlap between clusters." }` The selected value of $k$ had the highest average silhouette score among the values tested. This does not mean the clusters are completely separate or that another value outside the tested range would perform worse. Some overlap is reasonable given the short comments and similar vocabulary used across the threads. The selected value of $k=`r best_k`$ will be utilised consistently in Question 3(c) to fit the final K-means model.

## Question 3c. K-means Clustering and Cluster Interpretation

### Choice of Clustering Technique

I used K-means to group the comments based on their TF-IDF values. The document vectors were already L2-normalised in Question 3(b), so I used the same data for the final clustering.

K-means works by assigning comments to clusters and minimising the squared Euclidean distances between each comment and its cluster centre.

The objective function is:

$$
J = \sum_{j=1}^{k}
\sum_{\mathbf{x}_i \in C_j}
\|\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu}_j\|^2
$$

where:

- $C_j$ represents cluster $j$.
- $\mathbf{x}_i$ is the normalised TF-IDF vector of comment $i$.
- $\boldsymbol{\mu}_j$ is the centroid of cluster $j$.
- $k$ is the selected number of clusters.

I chose K-means because we covered this method in the subject and it works with numerical document vectors. I used $k=`r best_k`$, which gave the highest average silhouette score in Question 3(b).

The final model used the following parameters:

- `centers = best_k`: The selected number of clusters.
- `nstart = 25`: 25 random initialisations to reduce sensitivity to starting centroids.
- `iter.max = 300`: Maximum number of iterations per initialisation.
- `set.seed(42)`: Fixed random seed for reproducibility.

K-means uses squared Euclidean distance to form the clusters. Cosine distance was used separately to evaluate them using silhouette scores.

### 1. Fit the Final K-means Model

```{r q3c-final-kmeans, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Verify alignment with the original TF-IDF matrix
stopifnot(
  nrow(X_norm) == nrow(dtm),
  nrow(comment_metadata) == nrow(dtm),
  identical(rownames(X_norm), rownames(dtm)),
  identical(
    as.character(comment_metadata$comment_id),
    rownames(dtm)
  )
)

# Fit K-means using the same parameters as Question 3(b)
set.seed(42)

final_kmeans <- stats::kmeans(
  X_norm,
  centers = best_k,
  nstart = 25,
  iter.max = 300
)

# Calculate silhouette scores using cosine distance
final_silhouette <- cluster::silhouette(
  final_kmeans$cluster,
  cosine_dist
)

final_avg_silhouette <- mean(
  final_silhouette[, "sil_width"]
)

# Verify consistency with Question 3(b)
stopifnot(
  abs(final_avg_silhouette - best_score) < 1e-8
)

# Attach cluster labels to original comment metadata
cluster_assignments <- comment_metadata %>%
  mutate(
    cluster = factor(
      final_kmeans$cluster,
      levels = seq_len(best_k)
    ),
    silhouette = as.numeric(
      final_silhouette[, "sil_width"]
    )
  )

# Verify original comment alignment
stopifnot(
  nrow(cluster_assignments) == nrow(dtm),
  !anyDuplicated(cluster_assignments$comment_id),
  !anyNA(cluster_assignments$cluster),
  !anyNA(cluster_assignments$thread)
)

# Display model summary
model_summary <- tibble(
  Measure = c(
    "Number of comments",
    "Number of TF-IDF features",
    "Selected clusters",
    "Total within-cluster sum of squares",
    "Average silhouette score"
  ),
  Value = c(
    as.character(nrow(X_norm)),
    as.character(ncol(X_norm)),
    as.character(best_k),
    sprintf("%.4f", final_kmeans$tot.withinss),
    sprintf("%.4f", final_avg_silhouette)
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  model_summary,
  caption = "Final K-means clustering summary"
)
```

### 2. Examine Cluster Sizes

I counted the comments in each cluster to see how they were distributed across the groups.

```{r q3c-cluster-sizes}
cluster_sizes <- cluster_assignments %>%
  count(
    cluster,
    name = "n_comments",
    .drop = FALSE
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    percentage = round(
      100 * n_comments / sum(n_comments),
      2
    )
  )

knitr::kable(
  cluster_sizes,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Distribution of comments across clusters"
)
```

### 3. Identify Important Terms in Each Cluster

I calculated the average TF-IDF weight of each word across the comments in each cluster, including zero weights for comments where the word did not appear.

I used these averages to identify the words with the highest TF-IDF weights in each cluster and help interpret the differences between the groups.

```{r q3c-top-terms}
# Calculate the number of documents in each cluster
cluster_document_counts <- cluster_assignments %>%
  count(cluster, name = "n_documents")

# Calculate total TF-IDF weight for each term by cluster
cluster_terms <- tfidf_data %>%
  inner_join(
    cluster_assignments %>%
      select(comment_id, cluster),
    by = "comment_id"
  ) %>%
  group_by(cluster, word) %>%
  summarise(
    total_tfidf = sum(tf_idf),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    cluster_document_counts,
    by = "cluster"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    mean_tfidf = total_tfidf / n_documents
  ) %>%
  group_by(cluster) %>%
  slice_max(
    mean_tfidf,
    n = 10,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) %>%
  arrange(
    cluster,
    desc(mean_tfidf)
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(
    cluster,
    word,
    mean_tfidf
  )

knitr::kable(
  cluster_terms,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Top ten terms by mean TF-IDF weight in each cluster"
)
```

### 4. Examine Representative Comments

I selected five comments with the highest silhouette scores from each cluster to help understand what the groups were discussing.

These comments were more closely associated with their assigned clusters than with other clusters based on cosine distance. However, a high silhouette score does not necessarily mean a comment is closest to its cluster centre.

```{r q3c-representative-comments}
# Recover original comment text
original_comments <- replies %>%
  transmute(
    comment_id = as.character(uri),
    text
  ) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(comment_id),
    !is.na(text)
  ) %>%
  distinct(
    comment_id,
    .keep_all = TRUE
  )

# Join cluster assignments to original comments
cluster_examples <- cluster_assignments %>%
  left_join(
    original_comments,
    by = "comment_id"
  )

# Verify one-to-one matching
stopifnot(
  nrow(cluster_examples) == nrow(cluster_assignments),
  !anyNA(cluster_examples$text)
)

# Select five high-silhouette comments per cluster
representative_comments <- cluster_examples %>%
  group_by(cluster) %>%
  slice_max(
    silhouette,
    n = 5,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(
    cluster,
    desc(silhouette)
  )

knitr::kable(
  representative_comments %>%
    select(
      cluster,
      thread,
      silhouette,
      text
    ),
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Five high-silhouette comments from each cluster"
)
```

print(p_cluster_sizes)

### **Cluster Interpretation**

> The final K-means model divided `r nrow(cluster_assignments)` comments into `r best_k` clusters using L2-normalised TF-IDF vectors. The largest cluster contained `r max(cluster_sizes$n_comments)` comments, representing `r round(100 * max(cluster_sizes$n_comments) / nrow(cluster_assignments), 2)`% of the dataset. The smallest cluster contained `r min(cluster_sizes$n_comments)` comments. The average silhouette score was `r round(final_avg_silhouette, 4)`, which gives an indication of how well the clusters were separated using cosine distance. I looked at the highest-ranked TF-IDF words and representative comments to understand the content of each cluster. Some comments might still share similar vocabulary across different clusters, since K-means assigns every comment to a group even when the groups overlap. I kept the original thread labels and cluster assignments for the 2D visualisation in Question 3(d) and the comparison between threads and clusters in Question 3(e).

## Question 3d. Two-Dimensional Cluster Visualisation

### Purpose of the Visualisation

In Question 3(c), I used K-means to group comments based on their TF-IDF values. Since the TF-IDF matrix contains many words, I needed to reduce the data to two dimensions to display the clusters in a scatter plot.

I used truncated Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to reduce the normalised TF-IDF matrix to two dimensions.

In the plot, different colours represent the K-means clusters, while different shapes represent the original threads (T1, T2 and T3).

I kept the cluster assignments from Question 3(c) unchanged. SVD was only used to create the visualisation.

### 1. Prepare and Verify the Clustering Data

I used the same L2-normalised TF-IDF matrix (`X_norm`) from Question 3(c), along with the comment IDs, cluster assignments and thread labels stored in `cluster_assignments`.

I checked the comment IDs to make sure each plotted point matched the correct comment and its labels.

```{r q3d-prepare-data, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Verify that the normalised matrix and original DTM match
stopifnot(
  nrow(X_norm) == nrow(dtm),
  ncol(X_norm) == ncol(dtm),
  identical(
    rownames(X_norm),
    rownames(dtm)
  ),
  !is.null(rownames(X_norm)),
  !anyDuplicated(rownames(X_norm))
)

# Verify the original cluster assignments
stopifnot(
  all(
    c("comment_id", "thread", "cluster") %in%
      names(cluster_assignments)
  ),
  !anyDuplicated(cluster_assignments$comment_id),
  !anyNA(cluster_assignments$comment_id),
  !anyNA(cluster_assignments$thread),
  !anyNA(cluster_assignments$cluster)
)

# Match metadata to the exact matrix row order
plot_data <- cluster_assignments %>%
  slice(
    match(
      rownames(X_norm),
      comment_id
    )
  )

# Confirm correct document alignment
stopifnot(
  nrow(plot_data) == nrow(X_norm),
  !anyNA(plot_data$comment_id),
  identical(
    as.character(plot_data$comment_id),
    rownames(X_norm)
  ),
  all(
    as.character(plot_data$thread) %in%
      c("T1", "T2", "T3")
  ),
  dplyr::n_distinct(plot_data$cluster) == best_k
)

# Summarise the visualisation dataset
visual_summary <- tibble(
  Measure = c(
    "Total comments",
    "TF-IDF vocabulary features",
    "Number of K-means clusters",
    "Number of original threads"
  ),
  Value = c(
    nrow(X_norm),
    ncol(X_norm),
    dplyr::n_distinct(plot_data$cluster),
    dplyr::n_distinct(plot_data$thread)
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  visual_summary,
  caption = "Summary of the 2D visualisation dataset"
)
```

### 2. Reduce the TF-IDF Matrix to Two Dimensions

Truncated Singular Value Decomposition was applied to the L2-normalised TF-IDF matrix.

SVD decomposes a matrix $A$ as:

$$
A = U\Sigma V^T
$$

where:

- $U$ contains the left singular vectors associated with documents.
- $\Sigma$ contains the singular values.
- $V^T$ contains the right singular vectors associated with vocabulary features.

I kept the first two components and calculated the coordinates as:

$$
Z_2 = U_2\Sigma_2
$$

where $Z_2$ contains the coordinates of each comment along the first two SVD components.

SVD reduces the number of features while retaining some of the original data structure. Unlike standard PCA, truncated SVD does not require centring the data by subtracting the feature means.

```{r q3d-svd, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Check that the irlba package is available
if (!requireNamespace("irlba", quietly = TRUE)) {
  stop(
    "Please install irlba using install.packages('irlba')"
  )
}

# Ensure the matrix supports two-dimensional reduction
stopifnot(
  nrow(X_norm) > 2,
  ncol(X_norm) > 2
)

# Apply truncated SVD to the normalised TF-IDF matrix
set.seed(42)

svd_result <- irlba::irlba(
  X_norm,
  nv = 2,
  nu = 2
)

# Calculate two-dimensional document coordinates
coordinates <- sweep(
  svd_result$u,
  2,
  svd_result$d,
  FUN = "*"
)

colnames(coordinates) <- c(
  "SVD1",
  "SVD2"
)

# Verify coordinate dimensions and values
stopifnot(
  nrow(coordinates) == nrow(X_norm),
  ncol(coordinates) == 2,
  all(is.finite(coordinates))
)

# Calculate the proportion of total squared matrix
# magnitude represented by the first two components
component_proportions <- svd_result$d^2 /
  sum(X_norm^2)

svd_information <- tibble(
  Component = c(
    "SVD Component 1",
    "SVD Component 2",
    "Combined"
  ),
  Proportion = c(
    component_proportions[1],
    component_proportions[2],
    sum(component_proportions)
  ),
  Percentage = round(
    100 * c(
      component_proportions[1],
      component_proportions[2],
      sum(component_proportions)
    ),
    2
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  svd_information,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Proportion of squared TF-IDF matrix magnitude represented by the SVD components"
)
```

### 3. Combine Coordinates with Cluster and Thread Labels

I combined the two-dimensional coordinates with the original comment information.

Each point in the scatter plot represents one comment. Its colour shows the assigned K-means cluster, while its shape shows which thread the comment originally came from.

```{r q3d-combine-coordinates}
# Attach SVD coordinates to the aligned metadata
plot_data <- plot_data %>%
  mutate(
    SVD1 = coordinates[, 1],
    SVD2 = coordinates[, 2],
    cluster = factor(
      cluster,
      levels = as.character(seq_len(best_k))
    ),
    thread = factor(
      thread,
      levels = c("T1", "T2", "T3")
    )
  )

# Verify all labels and coordinates
stopifnot(
  !anyNA(plot_data$SVD1),
  !anyNA(plot_data$SVD2),
  !anyNA(plot_data$cluster),
  !anyNA(plot_data$thread),
  nrow(plot_data) == nrow(X_norm)
)

# Summarise comments by original thread
thread_visual_summary <- plot_data %>%
  count(
    thread,
    name = "n_comments",
    .drop = FALSE
  )

knitr::kable(
  thread_visual_summary,
  caption = "Comments included in the 2D visualisation by original thread"
)
```

### 4. Visualise the K-means Clusters in Two Dimensions

The scatter plot below shows the comments using the first two SVD components.

I used different colours for the K-means clusters and different shapes for the original threads (T1, T2 and T3).

The coordinates were calculated from the normalised TF-IDF matrix. I kept the original cluster assignments without running K-means again.

```{r q3d-visualisation, fig.width=11, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Two-dimensional truncated SVD projection of L2-normalised TF-IDF comments. Colours indicate K-means clusters and shapes indicate original thread labels."}
# Create the two-dimensional cluster visualisation
p_2d <- ggplot(
  plot_data,
  aes(
    x = SVD1,
    y = SVD2,
    colour = cluster,
    shape = thread
  )
) +
  geom_point(
    size = 2.2,
    alpha = 0.7,
    stroke = 0.4
  ) +
  scale_shape_manual(
    values = c(
      T1 = 16,
      T2 = 17,
      T3 = 15
    ),
    drop = FALSE
  ) +
  guides(
    colour = guide_legend(
      override.aes = list(
        size = 3,
        alpha = 1
      )
    ),
    shape = guide_legend(
      override.aes = list(
        size = 3,
        alpha = 1
      )
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "2D Visualisation of K-means Clusters",
    subtitle = paste(
      "Truncated SVD of normalised TF-IDF vectors, k =",
      best_k
    ),
    x = "SVD Component 1",
    y = "SVD Component 2",
    colour = "K-means Cluster",
    shape = "Original Thread"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "right",
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold"
    ),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

# Display the figure
print(p_2d)

# Save the figure
ggsave(
  "Data/q3_2d_clusters_threads.png",
  plot = p_2d,
  width = 11,
  height = 7,
  dpi = 300
)
```

### **Interpretation of the 2D Visualisation**

> The two-dimensional visualisation contains `r nrow(plot_data)` comments assigned to `r dplyr::n_distinct(plot_data$cluster)` K-means clusters and originating from `r dplyr::n_distinct(plot_data$thread)` discussion threads. The first two SVD components represent approximately `r round(100 * sum(component_proportions), 2)`% of the total squared magnitude of the normalised TF-IDF matrix. This measures how much of the original matrix is represented in two dimensions, rather than the percentage of centred variance explained by PCA. I used colours to identify the clusters and circles, triangles and squares to represent Threads T1, T2 and T3. Comments appearing close together have similar positions in the 2D plot. However, reducing the data to two dimensions loses some information, so the distances between points might differ from those in the original TF-IDF matrix. For this reason, I did not rely on the scatter plot alone to judge cluster quality. I also used the silhouette scores from Question 3(b), which were calculated using the original normalised TF-IDF vectors and cosine distances. In Question 3(e), I will compare the cluster assignments with the original thread labels to see how comments from each thread are distributed across the clusters.

### 5. Save the Visualisation Dataset

I saved the 2D coordinates, comment IDs, cluster assignments and thread labels so the visualisation results could be reproduced.

```{r q3d-save-coordinates, include=FALSE}
# Save the aligned visualisation dataset
readr::write_csv(
  plot_data,
  "Data/q3_2d_coordinates.csv"
)

# Verify saved outputs
stopifnot(
  file.exists("Data/q3_2d_coordinates.csv"),
  file.exists("Data/q3_2d_clusters_threads.png")
)
```

## Question 3e. Relationship Between Clusters and Original Threads

### Purpose of the Analysis

I compared the K-means clusters with the original Bluesky threads to see whether comments from the same thread were grouped together or spread across different clusters.

I used the cluster assignments from Question 3(c), without applying the additional short-comment filtering.

To compare Threads T1, T2 and T3, I created a contingency table, calculated percentages and used a stacked bar chart to show how comments were distributed across the clusters.

### 1. Prepare the Cluster Assignments

```{r q3e-prepare-data, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Use original assignments from Question 3(c)
cluster_assignments_e <- cluster_assignments %>%
  mutate(
    thread = factor(
      as.character(thread),
      levels = c("T1", "T2", "T3")
    ),
    cluster = factor(
      as.character(cluster),
      levels = as.character(seq_len(best_k))
    )
  )

# Verify original comment alignment
stopifnot(
  nrow(cluster_assignments_e) == nrow(dtm),
  identical(
    as.character(cluster_assignments_e$comment_id),
    rownames(dtm)
  ),
  !anyDuplicated(cluster_assignments_e$comment_id),
  !anyNA(cluster_assignments_e$thread),
  !anyNA(cluster_assignments_e$cluster),
  dplyr::n_distinct(cluster_assignments_e$thread) == 3,
  dplyr::n_distinct(cluster_assignments_e$cluster) == best_k
)

# Display dataset summary
dataset_summary_e <- tibble(
  Measure = c(
    "Total comments",
    "Original threads",
    "K-means clusters"
  ),
  Value = c(
    nrow(cluster_assignments_e),
    n_distinct(cluster_assignments_e$thread),
    n_distinct(cluster_assignments_e$cluster)
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  dataset_summary_e,
  caption = "Dataset summary for thread-cluster analysis"
)
```

### 2. Examine Cluster Membership Across Threads

I counted how many comments from each thread belonged to each cluster.

Since the threads contained different numbers of comments, I calculated percentages within each thread:

$$
P_{tj} = \frac{n_{tj}}{N_t}\times100
$$

where $n_{tj}$ is the number of comments from thread $t$ assigned to cluster $j$, and $N_t$ is the total number of comments in thread $t$.

```{r q3e-contingency-table}
# Create the thread-by-cluster contingency table
thread_cluster_table <- table(
  Thread = cluster_assignments_e$thread,
  Cluster = cluster_assignments_e$cluster
)

# Display observed counts
knitr::kable(
  as.data.frame.matrix(thread_cluster_table),
  caption = "Observed comment counts by thread and cluster"
)

# Calculate within-thread percentages
thread_cluster_pct <- prop.table(
  thread_cluster_table,
  margin = 1
) * 100

knitr::kable(
  round(
    as.data.frame.matrix(thread_cluster_pct),
    2
  ),
  caption = "Percentage of comments assigned to each cluster within each thread"
)

# Prepare tidy data for plotting
thread_clusters_e <- as.data.frame(
  thread_cluster_table
) %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  rename(
    thread = Thread,
    cluster = Cluster,
    n_comments = Freq
  ) %>%
  group_by(thread) %>%
  mutate(
    percentage = 100 * n_comments / sum(n_comments)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
```

### 3. Identify Dominant Clusters and Thread Concentration

I identified the cluster containing the most comments from each thread.

A higher percentage means more comments from the same thread were assigned to one cluster. However, if several threads share the same dominant cluster, this does not mean K-means has successfully separated the threads.

```{r q3e-dominant-clusters}
# Identify dominant cluster for each thread
thread_summary <- thread_clusters_e %>%
  group_by(thread) %>%
  slice_max(
    n_comments,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  transmute(
    thread,
    dominant_cluster = cluster,
    dominant_comments = n_comments,
    dominant_percentage = percentage
  )

# Count the clusters represented in each thread
thread_diversity <- thread_clusters_e %>%
  group_by(thread) %>%
  summarise(
    represented_clusters = sum(n_comments > 0),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Combine concentration and diversity results
thread_summary <- thread_summary %>%
  left_join(
    thread_diversity,
    by = "thread"
  )

knitr::kable(
  thread_summary,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Dominant clusters and cluster diversity by original thread"
)
```

### 4. Visualise Cluster Distribution Across Threads

I used a 100% stacked bar chart to compare the cluster distribution across T1, T2 and T3.

Each bar represents one thread, and the coloured sections show the percentage of comments assigned to each cluster.

Using percentages makes the three threads easier to compare, even when they contain different numbers of comments.

```{r q3e-thread-distribution-plot, fig.width=9, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Percentage distribution of K-means clusters across the three original Bluesky threads."}
p_threads <- ggplot(
  cluster_assignments_e,
  aes(
    x = thread,
    fill = cluster
  )
) +
  geom_bar(
    position = "fill",
    width = 0.7,
    colour = "white",
    linewidth = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent_format(
      accuracy = 1
    ),
    breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.2),
    expand = expansion(
      mult = c(0, 0)
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Cluster Distribution Across Original Threads",
    subtitle = "Proportion of comments assigned to each K-means cluster",
    x = "Original Discussion Thread",
    y = "Percentage of Comments",
    fill = "K-means Cluster"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "right",
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold"
    )
  )

print(p_threads)

ggsave(
  "Data/q3_thread_cluster_distribution.png",
  plot = p_threads,
  width = 9,
  height = 6,
  dpi = 300
)
```

### 5. Quantify the Relationship Between Threads and Clusters

I used a Pearson chi-square test to check whether the original thread labels were associated with the K-means cluster assignments.

The hypotheses were:

$$
H_0: \text{Cluster membership and original thread are independent.}
$$

$$
H_1: \text{Cluster membership and original thread are associated.}
$$

The test statistic is:

$$
\chi^2 =
\sum_{i=1}^{r}
\sum_{j=1}^{c}
\frac{(O_{ij}-E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}}
$$

where $O_{ij}$ is the observed number of comments, and $E_{ij}$ is the expected number if thread labels and cluster membership are independent.

I also calculated Cramér's V to measure the strength of the relationship:

$$
V =
\sqrt{
\frac{\chi^2}
{N\min(r-1,c-1)}
}
$$

Cramér's V ranges from 0 to 1. Values closer to zero indicate a weaker relationship between thread labels and cluster membership.

```{r q3e-association-test, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Perform Pearson chi-square test
chi_result <- suppressWarnings(
  chisq.test(
    thread_cluster_table,
    correct = FALSE
  )
)

# Calculate Cramer's V
N <- sum(thread_cluster_table)

cramers_v <- sqrt(
  as.numeric(chi_result$statistic) /
    (
      N * min(
        nrow(thread_cluster_table) - 1,
        ncol(thread_cluster_table) - 1
      )
    )
)

# Check expected frequencies
small_expected <- sum(
  chi_result$expected < 5
)

small_expected_pct <- 100 * mean(
  chi_result$expected < 5
)

# Summarise association results
association_results <- tibble(
  Measure = c(
    "Pearson chi-square statistic",
    "Degrees of freedom",
    "P-value",
    "Cramer's V",
    "Expected cells below 5 (%)"
  ),
  Value = c(
    sprintf("%.4f", unname(chi_result$statistic)),
    as.character(unname(chi_result$parameter)),
    format.pval(chi_result$p.value, digits = 4),
    sprintf("%.4f", cramers_v),
    sprintf("%.2f", small_expected_pct)
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  association_results,
  caption = "Association between original thread and cluster membership"
)
```

### **Interpretation**

> I compared `r nrow(cluster_assignments_e)` comments from three original threads across `r best_k` K-means clusters. The dominant cluster for Thread T1 was Cluster `r as.character(thread_summary$dominant_cluster[thread_summary$thread == "T1"])`, containing `r round(thread_summary$dominant_percentage[thread_summary$thread == "T1"], 2)`% of its comments. For Thread T2, the dominant cluster was Cluster `r as.character(thread_summary$dominant_cluster[thread_summary$thread == "T2"])`, containing `r round(thread_summary$dominant_percentage[thread_summary$thread == "T2"], 2)`%. For Thread T3, the dominant cluster was Cluster `r as.character(thread_summary$dominant_cluster[thread_summary$thread == "T3"])`, containing `r round(thread_summary$dominant_percentage[thread_summary$thread == "T3"], 2)`%. The chi-square test gave a statistic of `r round(unname(chi_result$statistic), 4)` with a p-value of `r format.pval(chi_result$p.value, digits = 4)`. `r if (chi_result$p.value < 0.05) {   "At the 5% significance level, the test indicates an association between original thread labels and cluster membership." } else {   "At the 5% significance level, the test does not provide sufficient evidence of an association between original thread labels and cluster membership." }` Cramér's V was `r round(cramers_v, 4)`, which measures how strongly the thread labels and clusters were associated. `r if (small_expected > 0) {   paste0(     "The contingency table contains ",     small_expected,     " expected cells below five (",     round(small_expected_pct, 2),     "%). The chi-square approximation should therefore be interpreted cautiously, particularly if expected frequencies are very small."   ) } else {   "All expected cell frequencies were at least five, supporting the use of the chi-square approximation." }` I used the contingency table and stacked bar chart to compare how comments from each thread were spread across the clusters. Even if the chi-square test shows an association, this does not necessarily mean K-means separated the three threads clearly. I also considered the dominant-cluster percentages and the amount of overlap between threads. The silhouette scores from Question 3(b) helped me assess how well the comments were separated based on their TF-IDF values. Since comments within the same discussion thread might be related, I treated the chi-square test as an exploratory comparison rather than definitive statistical evidence. Overall, I used these results to see whether the clusters reflected differences between the original threads or similarities in vocabulary across threads. The additional short-comment filtering analysis was kept separate to check whether comments with limited vocabulary affected the clustering results.
