## Supplementary Analysis: Sensitivity to Short-Comment Filtering

### Purpose of the Analysis

The main clustering analysis included all comments with nonzero TF-IDF values. However, comments with only a few words might not provide enough information for meaningful clustering.

I carried out an additional analysis to see whether removing comments with fewer than six terms with nonzero TF-IDF weights would affect the results.

I used the same K-means settings and cosine-distance silhouette scores as in Questions 3(b) and 3(c). This was an extra check, so the original clustering results remained the main findings.

This analysis is exploratory. The original clustering results remain the primary findings.

### 1. Filter Comments with Limited Vocabulary

I counted the number of terms with nonzero TF-IDF weights in each comment and kept only comments with at least six such terms.

After filtering, I removed vocabulary columns with no remaining nonzero values and normalised the document vectors using L2-normalisation.

```{r q3-supp-filter, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Count terms with nonzero TF-IDF weights per comment
document_lengths <- Matrix::rowSums(dtm != 0)

# Retain comments with at least six nonzero-weight terms
minimum_terms <- 6

dtm_filtered <- dtm[
  document_lengths >= minimum_terms,
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

# Remove vocabulary columns without remaining weights
dtm_filtered <- dtm_filtered[
  ,
  Matrix::colSums(dtm_filtered != 0) > 0,
  drop = FALSE
]

# Verify filtered matrix
stopifnot(
  nrow(dtm_filtered) > 10,
  ncol(dtm_filtered) > 0,
  !is.null(rownames(dtm_filtered)),
  !anyDuplicated(rownames(dtm_filtered)),
  all(Matrix::rowSums(dtm_filtered^2) > 0)
)

# Calculate L2 norms
filtered_norms <- sqrt(
  Matrix::rowSums(dtm_filtered^2)
)

# Normalise filtered document vectors
X_filtered <- as.matrix(
  Matrix::Diagonal(
    x = 1 / filtered_norms
  ) %*% dtm_filtered
)

# Preserve comment identifiers
rownames(X_filtered) <- rownames(dtm_filtered)

# Verify normalisation
stopifnot(
  all(abs(rowSums(X_filtered^2) - 1) < 1e-8)
)

# Summarise filtering
filter_summary <- tibble(
  Measure = c(
    "Original comments",
    "Filtered comments",
    "Excluded comments",
    "Comments retained (%)",
    "Original vocabulary terms",
    "Filtered vocabulary terms"
  ),
  Value = c(
    nrow(dtm),
    nrow(dtm_filtered),
    nrow(dtm) - nrow(dtm_filtered),
    round(100 * nrow(dtm_filtered) / nrow(dtm), 2),
    ncol(dtm),
    ncol(dtm_filtered)
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  filter_summary,
  caption = "Effect of short-comment filtering"
)
```

### 2. Evaluate Filtered Clustering Solutions

I ran K-means again on the filtered comments, testing values from $k=2$ to $k=10$.

For each value, I used 25 random starts, a maximum of 300 iterations and a fixed seed of 42, matching the original analysis.

I compared the average cosine-distance silhouette scores to see how well the filtered comments were separated. I also calculated the percentage of comments in the largest cluster to check whether one cluster contained most of the data.

```{r q3-supp-evaluation, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Calculate cosine distances
filtered_cosine_matrix <- pmax(
  1 - tcrossprod(X_filtered),
  0
)

filtered_cosine_matrix <- (
  filtered_cosine_matrix +
    t(filtered_cosine_matrix)
) / 2

diag(filtered_cosine_matrix) <- 0

filtered_cosine_dist <- stats::as.dist(
  filtered_cosine_matrix
)

# Identify the number of distinct document vectors
n_filtered_distinct <- nrow(
  unique(as.data.frame(X_filtered))
)

# Restrict candidate k to supported values
filtered_k_values <- 2:min(
  10,
  nrow(X_filtered) - 1,
  n_filtered_distinct - 1
)

stopifnot(
  length(filtered_k_values) > 0,
  best_k %in% filtered_k_values
)

# Fit each candidate once
filtered_models <- lapply(
  filtered_k_values,
  function(k) {

    set.seed(42)

    stats::kmeans(
      X_filtered,
      centers = k,
      nstart = 25,
      iter.max = 300
    )
  }
)

names(filtered_models) <- as.character(
  filtered_k_values
)

# Evaluate the fitted models
filtered_results <- purrr::map_dfr(
  filtered_k_values,
  function(k) {

    model <- filtered_models[[as.character(k)]]

    sil <- cluster::silhouette(
      model$cluster,
      filtered_cosine_dist
    )

    cluster_sizes_filtered <- table(
      factor(
        model$cluster,
        levels = seq_len(k)
      )
    )

    tibble(
      k = k,
      avg_silhouette = mean(
        sil[, "sil_width"]
      ),
      largest_cluster_pct = 100 *
        max(cluster_sizes_filtered) /
        length(model$cluster),
      total_wss = model$tot.withinss
    )
  }
)

# Select the highest-scoring filtered solution
best_filtered <- filtered_results %>%
  arrange(
    desc(avg_silhouette),
    k
  ) %>%
  slice_head(n = 1)

best_filtered_k <- best_filtered$k[[1]]

filtered_model <- filtered_models[[
  as.character(best_filtered_k)
]]

filtered_sil <- cluster::silhouette(
  filtered_model$cluster,
  filtered_cosine_dist
)

# Display candidate results
knitr::kable(
  filtered_results,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Silhouette evaluation of filtered K-means solutions"
)
```

### 3. Compare Original and Filtered Results

I first compared both datasets using the same number of clusters, $k=`r best_k`$, to see how filtering affected the silhouette scores.

I also found the best value of $k$ for the filtered dataset separately.

Since filtering changed the comments and vocabulary included in the analysis, I treated differences in silhouette scores as an indication of sensitivity rather than direct evidence of better clustering.

```{r q3-supp-comparison}
# Retrieve original results at the selected k
original_comparison <- silhouette_results %>%
  filter(k == best_k)

# Retrieve filtered results at the same k
filtered_comparison <- filtered_results %>%
  filter(k == best_k)

stopifnot(
  nrow(original_comparison) == 1,
  nrow(filtered_comparison) == 1
)

# Calculate largest cluster share for the original model
original_largest_pct <- 100 *
  max(table(final_kmeans$cluster)) /
  length(final_kmeans$cluster)

# Compare both datasets using the original k
comparison_table <- tibble(
  Dataset = c(
    "Original comments",
    "Filtered comments"
  ),
  Comments = c(
    nrow(dtm),
    nrow(X_filtered)
  ),
  Clusters = c(
    best_k,
    best_k
  ),
  Average_Silhouette = c(
    original_comparison$avg_silhouette,
    filtered_comparison$avg_silhouette
  ),
  Largest_Cluster_Pct = c(
    original_largest_pct,
    filtered_comparison$largest_cluster_pct
  )
)

# Calculate descriptive difference
silhouette_difference <-
  filtered_comparison$avg_silhouette -
  original_comparison$avg_silhouette

knitr::kable(
  comparison_table,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Original versus filtered clustering at the same k"
)

# Summarise the independently selected filtered solution
filtered_selection_summary <- tibble(
  Measure = c(
    "Original selected k",
    "Filtered selected k",
    "Best filtered silhouette score",
    "Silhouette difference at original k"
  ),
  Value = c(
    as.character(best_k),
    as.character(best_filtered_k),
    sprintf(
      "%.4f",
      best_filtered$avg_silhouette
    ),
    sprintf(
      "%+.4f",
      silhouette_difference
    )
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  filtered_selection_summary,
  caption = "Summary of filtered clustering results"
)
```

### 4. Examine Filtered Clusters and Representative Comments

I examined the filtered model with the highest average silhouette score.

I calculated the number of comments in each cluster and selected five comments with the highest silhouette scores from each group.

I used these comments to better understand the content of the filtered clusters.

```{r q3-supp-diagnostics, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Preserve filtered comment identifiers
filtered_assignments <- tibble(
  comment_id = rownames(X_filtered),
  cluster = factor(
    filtered_model$cluster,
    levels = seq_len(best_filtered_k)
  ),
  silhouette = as.numeric(
    filtered_sil[, "sil_width"]
  )
)

# Verify assignments
stopifnot(
  nrow(filtered_assignments) == nrow(X_filtered),
  identical(
    filtered_assignments$comment_id,
    rownames(X_filtered)
  ),
  !anyNA(filtered_assignments$cluster)
)

# Calculate filtered cluster sizes
filtered_sizes <- filtered_assignments %>%
  count(
    cluster,
    name = "n_comments",
    .drop = FALSE
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    percentage = round(
      100 * n_comments / sum(n_comments),
      2
    )
  )

knitr::kable(
  filtered_sizes,
  caption = "Distribution of filtered comments across clusters"
)

# Recover original text and thread labels
filtered_examples <- filtered_assignments %>%
  left_join(
    cluster_examples %>%
      select(
        comment_id,
        thread,
        text
      ),
    by = "comment_id"
  )

stopifnot(
  nrow(filtered_examples) == nrow(filtered_assignments),
  !anyNA(filtered_examples$text),
  !anyNA(filtered_examples$thread)
)

# Select five high-silhouette comments per cluster
representative_filtered <- filtered_examples %>%
  group_by(cluster) %>%
  slice_max(
    silhouette,
    n = 5,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(
    cluster,
    desc(silhouette)
  )

knitr::kable(
  representative_filtered %>%
    select(
      cluster,
      thread,
      silhouette,
      text
    ),
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Representative comments from the filtered clusters"
)
```

### 5. Visualise the Filtered Silhouette Results

The line chart below shows the average cosine-distance silhouette scores for the filtered dataset across different values of $k$.

The dashed vertical line marks the number of clusters with the highest score.

### **Interpretation**

> The original dataset contained `r nrow(dtm)` comments. After removing comments with fewer than six terms with nonzero TF-IDF weights, `r nrow(X_filtered)` comments remained, representing `r round(100 * nrow(X_filtered) / nrow(dtm), 2)`% of the original dataset. Using the same number of clusters, $k=`r best_k`$, the original dataset had an average silhouette score of `r round(original_comparison$avg_silhouette, 4)` compared with `r round(filtered_comparison$avg_silhouette, 4)` for the filtered dataset. `r if (silhouette_difference > 0) {   paste0(     "The filtered dataset produced a higher average silhouette score by ",     round(silhouette_difference, 4),     " at the same number of clusters."   ) } else if (silhouette_difference < 0) {   paste0(     "The filtered dataset produced a lower average silhouette score by ",     round(abs(silhouette_difference), 4),     " at the same number of clusters."   ) } else {   "Both datasets produced the same average silhouette score at the selected number of clusters." }` When I tested the number of clusters separately for the filtered dataset, the highest average silhouette score was `r round(best_filtered$avg_silhouette, 4)` at $k=`r best_filtered_k`$. The largest filtered cluster contained `r max(filtered_sizes$n_comments)` comments, representing `r round(max(filtered_sizes$percentage), 2)`% of the remaining dataset. These results show how removing comments with limited vocabulary affected the clustering. However, a higher silhouette score does not automatically mean the filtered clusters are more reliable, since filtering changes both the comments and vocabulary used in the analysis. I kept the original clustering results from Questions 3(a) to 3(e) as the main findings. This additional analysis helped me check how sensitive the results were to short comments.

## Question 4a. Identifying the Three Most Active Bluesky Users

```{r setup4, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 9, fig.height = 7, dpi = 160)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(igraph)
library(knitr)
```

### Methodology

I used the `atrrr` package to collect Bluesky posts about Bad Bunny's Super Bowl halftime performance.

I searched using four queries: `"Bad Bunny" halftime`, `"Bad Bunny" "Super Bowl"`, `"Benito" halftime`, and `"Bad Bunny"`. The searches covered posts published from 9 to 19 February 2026.

For each query, I requested up to 1,000 posts, sorted from newest to oldest. I then removed duplicate posts using their URIs and excluded posts outside the selected dates.

To keep the data relevant, I filtered for posts mentioning Bad Bunny or Benito along with terms related to the Super Bowl or halftime performance.

Finally, I identified users by their unique DIDs and counted how many different relevant posts each user had published. I ranked the users by their post counts to find the three most active accounts.

### R Code: Search Configuration

```{r q4a-search-settings}
end_date <- "2026-02-20"

  '"Benito" halftime',
  '"Bad Bunny"'
)

posts_per_query <- 1000L

# Original collection used:
# atrrr::search_post(
#   q = query,
#   since = start_date,
#   until = end_date,
#   sort = "latest",
#   limit = posts_per_query
# )
```

## Question 4b. Constructing and Visualising the Directed Follower Network

### Methodology

I used the three accounts identified in Question 4(a) to build a follower network.

Using the `atrrr` package, I requested up to 50 followers and 50 accounts followed by each user through `get_followers()` and `get_follows()`. If a request failed, I allowed up to three attempts.

I then used `igraph` to create a directed network. Each node represents a Bluesky account, identified by its DID. Each arrow points from the account following someone to the account being followed. For example, an arrow from User A to User B means User A follows User B.

Before creating the graph, I removed duplicate connections and self-loops, where an account would point to itself.

I highlighted the three selected accounts in orange and displayed the other accounts in blue. I used the Fruchterman-Reingold layout to arrange the nodes in the network plot.

### R Code: Network Collection

The R code below shows how I originally collected the follower and following data from Bluesky.

I did not run the API requests again when generating the report because the data had already been collected and saved.

```{r q4b-collection-code, eval=FALSE}
library(atrrr)
library(tidyverse)
library(igraph)

top_users <- read_csv(
  "Data/q4_top_three_users.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# API request with retries
safe_get <- function(actor, type, limit = 50L) {

  for (attempt in 1:3) {

    result <- tryCatch(
      {
        if (type == "followers") {
          atrrr::get_followers(
            actor = actor,
            limit = limit,
            verbose = FALSE
          )
        } else {
          atrrr::get_follows(
            actor = actor,
            limit = limit,
            verbose = FALSE
          )
        }
      },
      error = function(e) {
        message(
          actor, " / ", type, ": ",
          conditionMessage(e)
        )
        NULL
      }
    )

    if (!is.null(result)) {
      return(list(
        data = head(result, limit),
        status = "success"
      ))
    }

    Sys.sleep(2^attempt)
  }

  list(
    data = tibble(),
    status = "failed"
  )
}

edges_list <- list()
request_log <- list()

for (i in seq_len(nrow(top_users))) {

  actor <- top_users$author_did[i]
  handle <- top_users$author_handle[i]

  for (type in c("followers", "following")) {

    response <- safe_get(actor, type)
    result <- response$data

    request_log[[length(request_log) + 1]] <-
      tibble(
        actor = actor,
        handle = handle,
        type = type,
        status = response$status,
        retrieved = nrow(result)
      )

    if (
      nrow(result) == 0 ||
      !all(c("did", "actor_handle") %in% names(result))
    ) {
      next
    }

    if (type == "followers") {

      edges <- tibble(
        from = result$did,
        to = actor,
        from_handle = result$actor_handle,
        to_handle = handle
      )

    } else {

      edges <- tibble(
        from = actor,
        to = result$did,
        from_handle = handle,
        to_handle = result$actor_handle
      )
    }

    edges_list[[length(edges_list) + 1]] <- edges

    Sys.sleep(1.5)
  }
}

log_df <- bind_rows(request_log)

write_csv(
  log_df,
  "Data/q4_network_collection_log.csv"
)

if (length(edges_list) == 0) {
  stop("No network edges retrieved.")
}

edges <- bind_rows(edges_list) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(from),
    !is.na(to),
    from != to
  ) %>%
  distinct(from, to, .keep_all = TRUE)

write_csv(
  edges,
  "Data/q4_network_edges.csv"
)
```

### R Code: Constructing the Directed Network

The R code below loads the saved network data and rebuilds the directed graph without making any new API requests.

```{r q4b-network-graph}
# Load original collected data
top_users <- readr::read_csv(
  "Data/q4_top_three_users.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

network_edges <- readr::read_csv(
  "Data/q4_network_edges.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

network_log <- readr::read_csv(
  "Data/q4_network_collection_log.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Construct directed network
g <- igraph::graph_from_data_frame(
  network_edges %>%
    dplyr::select(from, to),
  directed = TRUE
)

# Remove isolated nodes, if present
g <- igraph::delete_vertices(
  g,
  which(igraph::degree(g, mode = "all") == 0)
)

# Identify the three selected users
igraph::V(g)$is_seed <-
  igraph::V(g)$name %in% top_users$author_did

# Calculate network size
network_summary <- data.frame(
  Metric = c("Nodes", "Directed edges"),
  Value = c(
    igraph::vcount(g),
    igraph::ecount(g)
  )
)
```

### Results

The network contained 196 nodes and 211 directed edges. All six API requests completed successfully.

The network plot shows the follower and following relationships connected to the three selected accounts. I highlighted these accounts in orange to make them easier to identify.

An incoming arrow means another account follows the selected user, while an outgoing arrow means the selected user follows another account.

All three accounts had 50 followers retrieved because I limited the collection to 50 per user. The number of followed accounts differed, with 46 for `webradiomexfm.bsky.social`, 13 for `tmspn.bsky.social` and two for `chartdata.xmirror.bot`.

The graph only represents the connections collected for this analysis, rather than the full Bluesky network. I collected the follower information in November 2026, so the relationships might have changed since the February 2026 discussion.

For this reason, I treated the network as a sample of the accounts' relationships at the time of collection, rather than a complete or historical record of their connections.

## Question 4c. Degree Centrality and PageRank Analysis

### Methodology

I used the `igraph` package to calculate centrality measures for the follower network from Question 4(b), which contained 196 accounts and 211 directed connections.

I calculated four measures for each account: in-degree, out-degree, total degree and PageRank.

In-degree counts how many accounts follow a user, while out-degree counts how many accounts the user follows. Total degree combines these two values.

PageRank measures an account's importance based on its incoming connections and the importance of the accounts linking to it. I used a damping factor of 0.85.

### R Code: Centrality Calculations

```{r q4c-centrality}
library(igraph)
library(tidyverse)

# 1. Load the original directed network
g <- readRDS("Data/q4_network_graph.rds")

top_users <- read_csv(
  "Data/q4_top_three_users.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

edges <- read_csv(
  "Data/q4_network_edges.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# 2. Create DID-to-handle lookup
handle_lookup <- bind_rows(
  edges %>% transmute(
    did = from,
    handle = from_handle
  ),
  edges %>% transmute(
    did = to,
    handle = to_handle
  ),
  top_users %>% transmute(
    did = author_did,
    handle = author_handle
  )
) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(did),
    !is.na(handle),
    handle != ""
  ) %>%
  distinct(did, .keep_all = TRUE)

# 3. Calculate centrality measures
centrality_results <- tibble(
  did = V(g)$name,
  in_degree = degree(
    g,
    mode = "in"
  ),
  out_degree = degree(
    g,
    mode = "out"
  ),
  total_degree = degree(
    g,
    mode = "all"
  ),
  pagerank = page_rank(
    g,
    directed = TRUE,
    damping = 0.85
  )$vector
) %>%
  left_join(
    handle_lookup,
    by = "did"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    handle = coalesce(handle, did)
  ) %>%
  select(
    did,
    handle,
    in_degree,
    out_degree,
    total_degree,
    pagerank
  )

# 4. Identify highest-ranking users
top_in_degree <- centrality_results %>%
  filter(in_degree == max(in_degree)) %>%
  arrange(handle)

top_out_degree <- centrality_results %>%
  filter(out_degree == max(out_degree)) %>%
  arrange(handle)

top_total_degree <- centrality_results %>%
  filter(total_degree == max(total_degree)) %>%
  arrange(handle)

top_pagerank <- centrality_results %>%
  filter(
    abs(pagerank - max(pagerank)) < 1e-12
  ) %>%
  arrange(handle)

# 5. Compare highest total degree and PageRank
same_top_user <- any(
  top_total_degree$did %in% top_pagerank$did
)

# 6. Create top-10 rankings
top10_degree <- centrality_results %>%
  arrange(desc(total_degree), handle) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)

top10_pagerank <- centrality_results %>%
  arrange(desc(pagerank), handle) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)
```

### Results

The three selected accounts had the same highest in-degree of 50.

```{r q4c-top-centrality}
knitr::kable(
  centrality_results %>%
    filter(did %in% top_users$author_did) %>%
    arrange(desc(total_degree)) %>%
    select(
      handle,
      in_degree,
      out_degree,
      total_degree,
      pagerank
    ),
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Table 6. Centrality Measures of the Three Selected Accounts",
  col.names = c(
    "Bluesky Account",
    "In-Degree",
    "Out-Degree",
    "Total Degree",
    "PageRank"
  )
)
```

### Highest-Ranking Accounts by Centrality Measure

```{r q4c-highest-users}
highest_users <- bind_rows(
  top_in_degree %>%
    mutate(metric = "In-degree"),
  top_out_degree %>%
    mutate(metric = "Out-degree"),
  top_total_degree %>%
    mutate(metric = "Total degree"),
  top_pagerank %>%
    mutate(metric = "PageRank")
) %>%
  select(
    metric,
    handle,
    in_degree,
    out_degree,
    total_degree,
    pagerank
  )

knitr::kable(
  highest_users,

  caption = "Table 7. Highest-Ranking Accounts by Centrality Measure",
  col.names = c(
    "Centrality Measure",
    "Bluesky Account",
    "In-Degree",
    "Out-Degree",
    "Total Degree",
    "PageRank"
  )
)
```

`webradiomexfm.bsky.social` ranked first for out-degree with 46 connections, total degree with 96 connections and PageRank with a score of approximately 0.108.

I also compared the accounts ranked first by total degree and PageRank. The comparison returned `TRUE`, confirming that `webradiomexfm.bsky.social` ranked highest for both measures.

### Discussion

The centrality results show that `webradiomexfm.bsky.social` occupied the highest-ranked position in the sampled network according to total degree and PageRank. The account had 50 incoming connections and 46 outgoing connections, giving a total degree of 96. The other two selected accounts had total degrees of 63 and 52.

Although the highest total-degree account also achieved the highest PageRank, the two measures assess different network properties. Degree centrality counts direct connections, while PageRank considers the importance of incoming connections. For example, `bsky.app` had a total degree of only two but ranked fourth by PageRank, with a score of approximately 0.0443. This demonstrates how an account with relatively few direct connections might achieve a higher PageRank through its position in the network.

The results are limited to the sampled network. In particular, the follower retrieval limit of 50 accounts per selected user affected the observed in-degree values. Therefore, the centrality rankings describe the collected network rather than the complete Bluesky network.


The results illustrate that `webradiomexfm.bsky.social` had the highest total degree and PageRank in the collected network.

This account had 50 incoming connections and 46 outgoing connections, giving a total degree of 96. The other two selected accounts had total degrees of 63 and 52.

Although the same account ranked first for both measures, degree centrality and PageRank measure different things. Degree centrality counts direct connections, while PageRank also considers the importance of accounts providing incoming connections.

For instance, `bsky.app` had only two direct connections but ranked fourth in PageRank, with a score of approximately 0.0443. This displays how an account with fewer connections might still receive a relatively high PageRank score.

These rankings only reflect the network I collected. Since I limited follower retrieval to 50 accounts per selected user, the observed in-degree values do not represent their full follower counts.

I therefore utilised these outcomes to compare the accounts within my sample rather than their overall importance across Bluesky.
